notes.meaning: The psalmist calls on God as the caring Shepherd who guides and guards His people like a flock. He pictures the Lord sitting as King above the golden cherubim on the ark of the covenant. From that holy throne, God is asked to shine out with His saving light and glory.

During the march through the wilderness, the tribes of Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh camped and marched right behind the ark of God. The writer asks the Lord to lead them once again and unleash His great power to rescue them from danger.

This repeated chorus asks God to restore His people to safety and peace. When God smiles and makes His face shine upon them with favour, darkness is driven away and deliverance comes. True safety never comes from human power, but only from God's gracious presence.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the prayer to be turned as an inward conversion of the heart, seeing God's hidden face as Christ's divinity veiled in human flesh.

notes.meaning: The people cry out because God seems silent and angry even while they are praying to Him. It feels as if His wrath is smoldering against their desperate pleas for help. Their greatest pain is not just their enemy's attacks, but the sense that God is displeased with them.

Sorrow has become like daily food and drink for God's suffering people. Instead of regular meals, they swallow continuous grief and weep bitter tears by the bowlful. Their misery is heavy and seems to have no end.

Neighboring countries quarrel over Israel and treat the nation like an easy prize to conquer. To make matters worse, their enemies mock them and laugh together over their helpless condition. They take joy in seeing God's chosen people brought low.

The chorus repeats the plea for help, but now calls upon God as the Lord of heaven's armies. Praying the same words again shows how deeply the people yearn for God's favour. Only the God who commands all the hosts of heaven has the power to save them.

Israel is compared to a tender grapevine that God dug up from Egypt and brought to a new home. To make room for it, the Lord drove out the idolatrous nations living in Canaan. God treated His people like a prized plant needing special care.

God prepared the soil of the promised land like a skilled gardener clearing out weeds and stones. Once planted there, Israel grew deep roots and quickly filled the land. The nation flourished and grew strong under God's blessing.

The vine grew so tall and wide that its shade covered the hills of Canaan. Its healthy branches stretched out as high and mighty as the great cedar trees. This shows how greatly God multiplied the nation in its best days.

The vine spread its branches west to the Mediterranean Sea and east to the Euphrates River. This fulfilled the large borders God had promised to Abraham and established during the reigns of David and Solomon. Israel had reached its fullest reach and glory.

The singer mourns that God has broken down the protective walls surrounding His vineyard. Without His defense, every passerby can freely reach in and steal the fruit. When God removes His shield, His people are left completely exposed to harm.

Cruel invaders are pictured as wild boars and forest beasts that tear up the vines and stomp the soil. Because God pulled back His protection, savage nations have trampled the once-fruitful land. The beauty of God's planting has been ruined.

The psalmist begs the God of heaven's armies to turn back and look down with mercy from heaven. Even though the people feel forgotten, they know God still sees their grief. They ask Him to visit this damaged vine and nurse it back to life.

The prayer asks God to guard the root and stock His own right hand planted. The vine is also described as the son whom God made strong for Himself, pointing to Israel as God's chosen child brought out of Egypt. They appeal to the special bond God made with them from the start.

The vine now lies cut down and burned with fire like useless waste. The people know this terrible loss came because God frowned on them in judgment for their sins. Without His favour, they perish under His stern rebuke.

The psalmist asks God to strengthen the man at His right hand, the leader God raised up to guide the nation. While this first applied to Israel's king or the nation as God's beloved son, Christian teachers have long seen it pointing to Jesus, the true Messiah who sits at God's right hand. With God's hand upholding their king, the people can find safety.

If God revives His people, they promise they will never turn back to idols or walk away from Him. Only God's grace can make dead hearts come alive so they can worship Him with true praise. Revived souls gladly cling to the Lord.

The psalm closes by repeating the chorus one last time, using God's fullest covenant name, the LORD God of hosts. This title reminds the people that the Almighty Creator rules every power in heaven and earth. When He smiles on them with forgiving love, they know they will be fully rescued.
